newsitem.title: USA: Strong holiday weekend helps stocks of retailers.
newsitem.headline: Strong holiday weekend helps stocks of retailers.

text.p: Retail stocks rose Monday as investors bet that strong holiday sales will lead the nation's stores to a better-than-expected fourth-quarter performance.
Analysts warned, however, that heavy consumer debt could dampen shoppers' spirits before spring.
"Investors are relieved to hear the shopping season is off to a good start," said N. Richard Nelson Jr, analyst at Nesbitt Burns "So far so good. The early scorecards are encouraging."
Improvements are easy after 1995's weak results, said Saul Yaari, senior retailing analyst at Piper Jaffray.

The stocks of most major retailers closed higher. Among the top gainers, Sears, Roebuck & Co. stock climbed $1.50 to $51.25. Federated Department Stores Inc. rose $1.625 to $35.75, while Gap Inc. gained $1.25 to $33.375.

Richard Giss, a partner at Deloitte & Touche's retail services group, said 464 retailers in the firm's annual holiday outlook survey expected profits to rise by 7.02 percent on average, more than double the 3.5 percent for the 1995 holiday season.
An average shop makes 25 percent of its year's profits during the holidays, while some retailers, such as gift shops, make as much as 40 percent, Giss said.

A strong job market, growing personal incomes and high consumer confidence were inspiring much of the increased spending, analysts said. But high consumer debt as a percentage of income was the major threat to the favourable trend, they said.
The debt loads could cause some "retrenchment" or a slowdown of retail spending in spring as shoppers attempt to pay off their credit card bills from the holidays, Yaari said.
Peter Schaeffer, an analyst at Dillon Read, said he was less bullish because many of the economic conditions behind the weak holiday last year were still present.
"It'll be a good Christmas, but not a great Christmas," Schaeffer said. Too many people are underemployed and, despite a good job market, job security is not too evident, he said.
He said retailers tended to "exaggerate" holiday figures, but Thursday's reports of retail sales for November should give a clearer figure.
Toys, jewelry and high-end apparel should show strong sales growth, while consumer electronics and furniture will be weak, and furnishing and shoes will finish up slightly, analysts said.

Last year, weak October sales led to sharp markdowns and a bleak holiday shopping season that hurt fourth-quarter profits, Yaari said. He said leaner inventories have helped retailers limit their markdowns this year and helped boost profits.
